title: Galactic soup
caption: The interacting galaxy pair Zw I 136 and its neighbors, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: 2MASX J16133219+5103436, SDSS J161330.18+510335, Zw I 136 · constellation Hercules
credit: Image credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA Acknowledgement: Judy Schmidt

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Galaxies of many colors and shapes crowd this Hubble frame. Some are bright and nearby, some are fuzzy, and some are so far off that they show up only as small specks. The two on the left stand out. At the bottom is 2MASX J16133219+5103436, and above it is its blue-tinted companion SDSS J161330.18+510335.

Together the two form a pair called Zw I 136. The upper galaxy is slightly closer to us, but they are near enough to each other to interact. Both have disturbed shapes and extended soft halos, unlike the third bright object in the frame, a spiral seen edge-on toward the right.

Pairs like this help with a central question in the study of how galaxies change over time. Astronomers want to know how encounters between galaxies set off waves of star formation, and why that star formation then stops abruptly.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed this field in ultraviolet, blue and red light. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The ultraviolet filter records light the eye cannot see, and these galaxies are far too faint to see without a large telescope.

explore: Astronomers sort galaxies by their appearance and shape. The best-known scheme is the Hubble sequence, devised by Edwin Hubble. Judy Schmidt entered a version of this picture into the Hubble's Hidden Treasures image processing competition.
alt: Many galaxies of different colors and shapes, with two disturbed galaxies on the left, the upper one blue-tinted, and an edge-on spiral on the right.
